related_questions.question: How do you treat a hemiplegic migraine?

text_blocks.snippet: Hemiplegic migraine treatment focuses on both acute management of attacks and prevention of future episodes, often involving a combination of medications and lifestyle adjustments. Treatment plans are highly individualized and should be developed in consultation with a headache specialist or neurologist experienced in treating this rare condition.
snippet_highlighted_words: focuses on both acute management of attacks and prevention of future episodes, often involving a combination of medications and lifestyle adjustments

list.title: Pain Relief:
list.snippet: Medications like NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) or acetaminophen are often used first-line for pain management.

list.title: Nausea Relief:
list.snippet: Anti-nausea medications may be prescribed to address nausea and vomiting, which can accompany hemiplegic migraines.

list.title: Triptans:
list.snippet: While controversial due to potential vasoconstrictive effects, triptans (e.g., almotriptan, eletriptan, sumatriptan) may be used cautiously during the headache phase if other treatments are insufficient.

list.title: Intranasal Ketamine:
list.snippet: Some individuals may benefit from intranasal ketamine, particularly to shorten the duration of aura.

list.title: Verapamil:
list.snippet: Intravenous verapamil has shown promise in quickly resolving symptoms and may be used in acute settings.

list.title: Corticosteroids:
list.snippet: Corticosteroids may be considered for prolonged hemiplegic migraine attacks.
Calcium Channel Blockers: Verapamil, flunarizine are commonly used.
Antidepressants: Tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline) and SNRIs may be prescribed.
Anti-Seizure Medications: Topiramate, valproic acid are sometimes used.
CGRP Antagonists: A newer class of medications that can help prevent migraines.
Botox: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) injections may be used to prevent chronic migraines, including hemiplegic migraines.
Acetazolamide: May be considered, particularly for familial hemiplegic migraine.
Trigger Avoidance: Identifying and avoiding individual triggers, such as specific foods, stress, or sleep disturbances, is crucial.
Regular Sleep Schedule: Maintaining a consistent sleep schedule is important.
Stress Management: Techniques like exercise, meditation, or therapy can help manage stress.
Diet: A balanced and nutritious diet, along with adequate hydration, is recommended.

list.title: Neuromodulation Devices:
list.snippet: Devices like Nerivio, Cefaly, Relivion, gammaCore, and SAVI Dual can be used to deliver electrical or magnetic impulses to nerves or areas of the brain involved in migraine, potentially reducing or preventing attacks.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Hemiplegic migraines can be difficult to diagnose and may require specialized testing and evaluation by a neurologist.

list.title: Individualized Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment plans should be tailored to the individual's specific symptoms, triggers, and medical history.

list.title: Genetic Testing:
list.snippet: Genetic testing may be considered to identify gene mutations associated with familial hemiplegic migraine, but it doesn't change treatment approaches.

list.title: Ongoing Management:
list.snippet: Hemiplegic migraines may not be curable, but with proper treatment and management, individuals can experience fewer and less severe attacks.
